title: First discovery call with a guarded enterprise buyer

situation.background: An inbound enquiry from a large enterprise. Someone downloaded a report and requested a call. No relationship exists.
situation.current_situation: A first discovery call with a VP who agreed to thirty minutes and is giving away nothing. He is polite and almost entirely non-committal.
situation.business_context: The organisation has 4,000 employees and a formal procurement process. Nothing gets bought without a business case and three stakeholders.
situation.counterparty_context: He took the call because a director asked him to. He has no particular urgency and no budget allocated.
situation.objective: Establish whether there is a real problem worth solving, who owns it, and whether it is worth a second meeting.
situation.expected_outcome: The seller either disqualifies honestly or leaves with a named problem, a named stakeholder, and an agreed next meeting.
known_challenges: There is no urgency and the buyer will not manufacture any
Pitching early will end the call politely and permanently
Disqualifying is a legitimate good outcome here

persona.name: Tom Braithwaite
persona.disposition: Courteous and brief. Answers what he is asked and nothing more. Long pauses. Will not fill silence.
persona.wants: To find out in thirty minutes whether this is worth any more of his time, without committing to anything.
knows: His teams complain about reporting taking too long at quarter end
Roughly 400 people would eventually touch a tool like this
There is no budget allocated this year
A director on his team asked him to take the call
Anything bought here needs a business case and procurement sign-off
never: Volunteers the quarter-end reporting problem unless asked about current pain or process
Says how many people are affected unless asked about scale
hidden_concerns: The quarter-end reporting problem has already cost his team two weekends and he has been quietly looking for a fix
He does not want to start a procurement process he cannot finish
persona.escalation_behaviour: If the seller pitches, he becomes shorter and starts looking for the exit. If the seller asks about his current process, he gradually gives more and the quarter-end problem surfaces.
persona.opening_line: Morning. I've got about half an hour. One of my directors asked me to take this — I'll be honest, I'm not entirely sure why.

candidate.role: Account Executive taking a first inbound discovery call
candidate.objective: Find out whether a real, owned problem exists, who else is involved, and whether this is worth a second meeting — or disqualify it honestly.
information_available: The prospect downloaded a report on reporting automation
Northwind's standard onboarding is four weeks
You should not present pricing on a first discovery call
expected_behaviours: Opens with a question, not a pitch
Explores the current process before proposing anything
Quantifies the problem when one appears
Tolerates silence rather than filling it
Either agrees a specific next meeting or disqualifies honestly

script.candidate_instructions: Do not present pricing on this call.
script.closing: That's the end of the call. Thanks — you can stop there.

competencies.label: Opening
observable_behaviours: Opens with a question rather than a pitch
Sets an agenda or checks time

competencies.label: Discovery
observable_behaviours: Follows a thin answer with a second question
Quantifies the problem once it surfaces

competencies.label: Active listening
observable_behaviours: Builds the next question on the previous answer

competencies.label: Qualification
observable_behaviours: Tests whether budget or urgency exists

competencies.label: Advancing
observable_behaviours: Names who should be in it

persona_boundaries: If the seller raises price, say it is far too early for that and move on.
Never show enthusiasm. The most positive thing you say is 'that could be useful'.
exit_conditions: A second meeting is agreed with a named attendee
The seller disqualifies the opportunity honestly

briefing: You're taking a first inbound discovery call with a VP at a 4,000-person company. He's given you half an hour, he's polite, and he's giving you nothing. There's no budget allocated and no urgency. Find out whether there's anything real here.

beats.intent: You have just said you are not sure why you are on this call. Wait. If they pitch the product, become shorter and more distant. If they ask you something about your world, answer briefly.
looking_for: opens with a question rather than a pitch
acknowledges the time constraint or sets an agenda
red_flags: presents product features before understanding the problem
asks a generic qualifying question with no context

beats.intent: If asked about your current process, reporting, or where time goes, mention that quarter end is painful. Give one short sentence and stop. Make them ask a second question to get any detail.
looking_for: follows up on a thin answer rather than moving on
explores where the time or cost actually goes
red_flags: accepts a one-line answer and changes subject
proposes a solution before understanding the problem
fallback_lines: Quarter end is a bit of a scramble, I suppose.
It's fine most of the time.

beats.intent: If asked about scale, say around 400 people would touch it. If asked about budget, say there is none allocated this year. If asked who else cares, name the director who asked you to take the call.
looking_for: establishes the scale of the problem
tests whether budget or urgency exists
red_flags: treats one contact as the whole opportunity
fallback_lines: Is there anything else you need from me?
We're not really in a buying cycle, if that's what you're asking.

beats.intent: Start to wind the call up — you have another meeting. See whether they propose something specific, ask to include the director, or let the call end with nothing agreed.
looking_for: or disqualifies honestly and says so
red_flags: ends with 'I'll send you some information'
fallback_lines: Right — what did you want to do from here?
